Pattern 1: Environment-Driven Backend Switching ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • The same codebase must deliver real email in production but capture email in development, test, and CI.
  • Backend configuration arrives from environment variables (or a config service) that differ per environment.
  • You want a single, explicit, fail-fast decision point instead of scattered NODE_ENV checks.

Complete Example ​

The MailFactoryConfig type discriminator ("smtp" | "memory") turns the environment decision into one configuration object that createMailProvider() maps to a concrete provider:

typescript
import {
    createMailProvider,
    type MailFactoryConfig,
    type MailProvider,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

/** Read a required environment variable or fail with a clear message. */
function requireEnv(name: string): string {
    const value = process.env[name];
    if (!value) {
        throw new Error(`Missing required environment variable: ${name}`);
    }
    return value;
}

/**
 * Environment-driven mailer factory.
 * Production uses SMTP; dev, test, and CI capture mail in memory.
 */
function buildMailer(): MailProvider {
    const isProduction = process.env.NODE_ENV === "production";

    const config: MailFactoryConfig = isProduction
        ? {
              type: "smtp",
              host: requireEnv("SMTP_HOST"),
              port: Number(process.env.SMTP_PORT ?? "587"),
              secure: process.env.SMTP_SECURE === "true",
              auth: {
                  user: requireEnv("SMTP_USER"),
                  pass: requireEnv("SMTP_PASS"),
              },
          }
        : {
              type: "memory",
              serviceName: "dev-mailer",
          };

    const mailer = createMailProvider(config);
    console.log(`Mailer "${mailer.serviceName}" created for the ${config.type} backend`);
    return mailer;
}

const mailer = buildMailer();

const result = await mailer.send({
    from: "noreply@example.com",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Your order shipped",
    text: "Your order is on its way.",
});

console.log("Accepted:", result.accepted);
console.log("Message ID:", result.messageId);

await mailer.shutdown();

Running with NODE_ENV unset produces the memory backend and prints something like:

text
Mailer "dev-mailer" created for the memory backend
Accepted: [ 'customer@example.com' ]
Message ID: <memory-1732000000000-0@test>

Why This Pattern Matters ​

Without a factory, the environment decision is duplicated at every construction site, and missing configuration only surfaces when the first email fails to send:

typescript
// ✗ Before — the decision leaks everywhere and nothing validates the config:
const mailer =
    process.env.NODE_ENV === "production"
        ? new SmtpMailProvider({ host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587 })
        : new MemoryMailProvider();

createMailProvider() collapses that decision into one place. In a WebAFX application the resulting provider is registered exactly like a hand-built one — the environment logic never leaves the bootstrap module:

typescript
// WebAFX bootstrap — the backend was selected once, at startup:
app.use(createMailPlugin(buildMailer()));

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • Validate before constructing. createMailProvider() forwards host and port to the SMTP transport without validating them. An empty SMTP_HOST produces a provider that fails on its first send(); the requireEnv() helper turns that into a startup error instead.
  • Unknown types fail fast. If type comes from untyped JSON or a bad environment value, the factory throws Unknown mail type: "<value>". Supported types: "smtp", "memory". — catch it during bootstrap, not on the first request.
  • The memory branch ignores SMTP fields. When type: "memory", host/port/auth are never read, so partial configuration is harmless in non-production environments.
  • Lifecycle still applies. The WebAFX plugin calls shutdown() for you; standalone code must call await mailer.shutdown() explicitly (memory shutdown() clears captured messages, SMTP closes the connection pool).

Pattern 2: Multiple Named Mailers ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • Transactional mail (receipts, password resets) and marketing/bulk mail should not share a relay, credential set, or sending reputation.
  • Different parts of the application genuinely need different transports or service identities.
  • You want each mailer to appear as its own singleton service with its own health entry and shutdown path.

Complete Example ​

The service name — defaulting to "mailer" — is the registration key. Overriding it per provider makes multiple mailers coexist cleanly:

typescript
import {
    createMailPlugin,
    MemoryMailProvider,
    SmtpMailProvider,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Transactional mail — high-deliverability relay, sends order receipts.
const transactionalMailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    serviceName: "transactional-mailer",
    host: "smtp.transactional.example.com",
    port: 587,
    auth: { user: "tx@example.com", pass: "tx-secret" },
});

// Marketing mail — bulk relay with a separate reputation.
const marketingMailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    serviceName: "marketing-mailer",
    host: "smtp.marketing.example.com",
    port: 587,
    auth: { user: "mkt@example.com", pass: "mkt-secret" },
});

// Development/test capture under its own name.
const devMailer = new MemoryMailProvider({ serviceName: "dev-mailer" });

const plugins = [
    createMailPlugin(transactionalMailer),
    createMailPlugin(marketingMailer),
    createMailPlugin(devMailer, { priority: 20 }),
];

for (const plugin of plugins) {
    console.log(`Plugin "${plugin.name}" (priority ${plugin.priority})`);
}

// Each mailer sends independently:
await transactionalMailer.send({
    from: "receipts@example.com",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Your receipt",
    text: "Thanks for your purchase.",
});

await marketingMailer.send({
    from: "news@example.com",
    to: ["subscriber-1@example.com", "subscriber-2@example.com"],
    subject: "This month at Example Corp",
    text: "Here is what is new.",
});

await devMailer.send({
    from: "noreply@example.com",
    to: "developer@example.com",
    subject: "Preview",
    text: "Rendered in memory only.",
});

console.log("Last captured dev email:", devMailer.getLastMessage()?.message.subject);

// Shut down every provider explicitly in standalone usage:
await Promise.all([
    transactionalMailer.shutdown(),
    marketingMailer.shutdown(),
    devMailer.shutdown(),
]);

In a WebAFX application, each plugin registers its own singleton service; resolution happens by name:

typescript
// Bootstrap — three plugins, three singleton services:
app.use(createMailPlugin(transactionalMailer));
app.use(createMailPlugin(marketingMailer));
app.use(createMailPlugin(devMailer, { priority: 20 }));

// Anywhere in the app — resolve the mailer you mean, by name:
const receipts = services.get<MailProvider>("transactional-mailer");

await receipts.send({
    from: "receipts@example.com",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Your receipt",
    text: "Thanks for your purchase.",
});

Why This Pattern Matters ​

This pattern is about failure isolation and identity:

  • Reputation and credential isolation — a throttled or compromised marketing relay cannot take down password resets, and vice versa.
  • Uniform typing — every mailer is a MailProvider, so shared helpers (the retry wrapper from Pattern 5, the guarded send wrapper from Pattern 7) accept any of them unchanged.
  • Independent lifecycle — each plugin registers its own singleton and returns its own health/shutdown hooks, so health checks and disposal cover every mailer.
  • Explicit call sites — resolving by name means no code silently depends on a single global "mailer"; the choice is visible at the call site.

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • Service names must be unique. The plugin name equals provider.serviceName; two providers that both default to "mailer" collide on the same container key. Override serviceName for every additional mailer.
  • Each SMTP provider owns a transport and its own connection pool. More mailers mean more sockets and memory; keep the number small and justified.
  • Shut down every provider. Plugins dispose their provider during application shutdown; standalone code must call shutdown() per mailer, as shown above.
  • Priority controls install order only. Health reporting and service resolution are independent of plugin priority; use it purely for ordering relative to other plugins.

Pattern 3: Custom Backends via Subclassing ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • You need a backend the package does not ship — an audit log, a local outbox, an HTTP-API transport, or a console logger for local development.
  • You want to wrap a built-in provider with cross-cutting behavior (auditing, metrics, rate limiting) without touching call sites.
  • You want the custom backend to participate in the same plugin infrastructure — singleton registration, health hook, shutdown hook — as the built-ins.

Complete Example ​

Because MailProvider and createMailPlugin() are both public, a decorator provider gets the full plugin lifecycle for free. This example records every send attempt to a JSON Lines audit file before delegating to the wrapped provider:

typescript
import { appendFile } from "node:fs/promises";

import {
    MailProvider,
    MemoryMailProvider,
    createMailPlugin,
    type MailMessage,
    type MailProviderConfig,
    type MailResult,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

/**
 * Decorator provider that records every send attempt to an audit log
 * (JSON Lines), then delegates to the wrapped provider.
 */
class AuditingMailProvider extends MailProvider {
    private readonly inner: MailProvider;
    private readonly logPath: string;

    constructor(inner: MailProvider, logPath: string, config: MailProviderConfig = {}) {
        super(config);
        this.inner = inner;
        this.logPath = logPath;
    }

    async send(message: MailMessage): Promise<MailResult> {
        const entry = {
            at: new Date().toISOString(),
            from: message.from,
            to: message.to,
            subject: message.subject,
        };

        try {
            const result = await this.inner.send(message);
            await appendFile(
                this.logPath,
                JSON.stringify({ ...entry, outcome: "sent", messageId: result.messageId }) + "\n"
            );
            return result;
        } catch (error) {
            const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown error";
            await appendFile(
                this.logPath,
                JSON.stringify({ ...entry, outcome: "failed", reason }) + "\n"
            );
            throw error;
        }
    }

    async health(): Promise<boolean> {
        return this.inner.health();
    }

    async shutdown(): Promise<void> {
        await this.inner.shutdown();
    }
}

const baseMailer = new MemoryMailProvider();

const auditedMailer = new AuditingMailProvider(baseMailer, "./mail-audit.jsonl", {
    serviceName: "audited-mailer",
});

const result = await auditedMailer.send({
    from: "billing@example.com",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Invoice 1042",
    text: "Your invoice is attached.",
});

console.log("Accepted:", result.accepted);

// The plugin layer accepts custom providers exactly like the built-ins:
const plugin = createMailPlugin(auditedMailer);
console.log(`Plugin "${plugin.name}" (priority ${plugin.priority})`);

await auditedMailer.shutdown();

Because the plugin layer trusts the contract rather than the implementation, a custom provider must honor the same semantics. The package verifies both built-in backends with one shared contract suite (see tests/abstract-contract.test.ts); run the same idea against your backend in your own test project:

typescript
import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import {
    MemoryMailProvider,
    type MailProvider,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

/**
 * Run the shared contract against any provider factory.
 * Call it once per backend — built-in or custom.
 */
function describeMailProviderContract(
    name: string,
    createProvider: () => MailProvider
): void {
    describe(`MailProvider contract: ${name}`, () => {
        it("returns a result with the recipient in accepted", async () => {
            const provider = createProvider();
            try {
                const result = await provider.send({
                    from: "contract@example.com",
                    to: "recipient@example.com",
                    subject: "Contract",
                    text: "Contract check",
                });

                expect(result.accepted).toContain("recipient@example.com");
                expect(Array.isArray(result.rejected)).toBe(true);
                if (result.messageId !== undefined) {
                    expect(typeof result.messageId).toBe("string");
                    expect(result.messageId.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
                }
            } finally {
                await provider.shutdown();
            }
        });

        it("reports health as a boolean and defaults the service name to 'mailer'", async () => {
            const provider = createProvider();
            try {
                expect(typeof (await provider.health())).toBe("boolean");
                expect(provider.serviceName).toBe("mailer");
            } finally {
                await provider.shutdown();
            }
        });
    });
}

describeMailProviderContract("MemoryMailProvider", () => new MemoryMailProvider());

// Your custom backend joins the same suite in your own tests:
// describeMailProviderContract(
//     "AuditingMailProvider",
//     () => new AuditingMailProvider(new MemoryMailProvider(), "./audit.jsonl")
// );

Why This Pattern Matters ​

  • Open for extension, closed for modification. The abstract class is exported precisely so new transports can be added without forking the package, and createMailPlugin() wires any MailProvider — SMTP, memory, or yours — into the same singleton-service, health, and shutdown infrastructure.
  • Decorators separate concerns. Call sites keep calling send(); auditing, metrics, or fallback routing are added once, around the provider, instead of in every sending module.
  • Behavioral parity is testable. A shared contract suite makes "indistinguishable from the built-ins" a checkable property rather than a hope — the exact approach the package uses for its own two backends.

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • Implement all three members. TypeScript strict mode enforces send(), health(), and shutdown() at compile time.
  • Match the error model. send() should throw on failure (like SmtpMailProvider) so application-level retry and error handling behave identically; health() should never throw — catch internally and return a boolean.
  • Make shutdown() idempotent. The plugin wires provider.shutdown() into both the singleton service's dispose hook and the returned shutdown hook, so teardown paths can invoke it more than once:
typescript
private disposed = false;

async shutdown(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.disposed) {
        return;
    }
    this.disposed = true;
    await this.inner.shutdown();
}
  • Watch the send-path latency. Awaiting audit I/O adds a disk write to every send(); for hot paths, buffer writes or make them fire-and-forget with their own error handling.

Pattern 4: Deterministic Email Testing ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • Unit-testing services or controllers that send email.
  • Asserting on content, recipients, and result metadata of outgoing mail without a mail server.
  • Integration-testing a WebAFX application where email is a side effect you want to observe and verify.

Complete Example ​

The memory backend stores every send as a SentMailEntry ({ message, result }). Combined with constructor injection, this makes email assertions trivial:

typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import { MemoryMailProvider, type MailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

/** Application service with constructor-injected mailer — trivially testable. */
class RegistrationService {
    constructor(private readonly mailer: MailProvider) {}

    async register(email: string): Promise<void> {
        await this.mailer.send({
            from: "noreply@example.com",
            to: email,
            subject: "Welcome aboard!",
            text: "Your account is ready.",
            html: "<p>Your account is <strong>ready</strong>.</p>",
        });
    }
}

describe("RegistrationService", () => {
    let mailer: MemoryMailProvider;
    let service: RegistrationService;

    beforeEach(() => {
        mailer = new MemoryMailProvider();
        service = new RegistrationService(mailer);
    });

    afterEach(async () => {
        // shutdown() clears the store — always run it AFTER assertions.
        await mailer.shutdown();
    });

    it("sends exactly one welcome email with the right content", async () => {
        await service.register("new-user@example.com");

        const sent = mailer.getSentMessages();
        expect(sent).toHaveLength(1);
        expect(sent[0].message.to).toBe("new-user@example.com");
        expect(sent[0].message.subject).toBe("Welcome aboard!");
        expect(sent[0].result.accepted).toEqual(["new-user@example.com"]);
        expect(sent[0].result.rejected).toEqual([]);
        expect(sent[0].result.messageId).toMatch(/^<memory-\d+-\d+@test>$/);
    });

    it("clears captures between cases without recreating the provider", async () => {
        await service.register("first@example.com");
        mailer.clear();

        await service.register("second@example.com");

        expect(mailer.getSentMessages()).toHaveLength(1);
        expect(mailer.getLastMessage()?.message.to).toBe("second@example.com");
    });
});

When the application runs under WebAFX, the one-liner memoryMailPlugin() hides the provider instance, so there is no handle to assert with. Own the provider instead:

typescript
// Before — the provider lives inside the plugin;
// there is no handle for getSentMessages() in application tests.
app.use(memoryMailPlugin());
typescript
// After — own the provider, wrap it, keep the handle:
const mailer = new MemoryMailProvider({ serviceName: "mailer" });
app.use(createMailPlugin(mailer));

// Exercise the application (HTTP calls, jobs, etc.), then assert:
expect(mailer.getSentMessages()).toHaveLength(1);

// Teardown last — shutdown() clears the captured messages.
await mailer.shutdown();

The memory backend cannot fail, so failure-path tests need a stub. Subclass MailProvider (a plain object literal is not assignable — the base class has protected members):

typescript
// MemoryMailProvider.send() never throws — to exercise failure handling,
// subclass MailProvider with a stub that fails on demand:
class FailingMailProvider extends MailProvider {
    async send(message: MailMessage): Promise<MailResult> {
        throw new Error(`Simulated SMTP failure for "${message.subject}"`);
    }

    async health(): Promise<boolean> {
        return false;
    }

    async shutdown(): Promise<void> {
        // No resources to release in this stub.
    }
}

Why This Pattern Matters ​

  • Zero infrastructure. Full email flows run in CI without Docker, without a fake SMTP server, and without network access.
  • Full observability. Each entry pairs the original message with the result that send() returned, so tests can assert on input and output in one place.
  • Predictable identifiers. Message IDs follow the deterministic <memory-${Date.now()}-${index}@test> shape, safe to match with a regex instead of brittle exact strings.
  • Reference fidelity. Entries store the original message object, so identity assertions (expect(stored.message).toBe(originalMessage)) hold — the same guarantee the package's own tests rely on.

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • Assert before teardown. shutdown() clears the store (it delegates to clear()). If you shut down in afterEach, all assertions must run inside the test body — never after cleanup.
  • Captures are by reference, not deep clones. If code under test mutates a MailMessage object after send(), the stored entry reflects that mutation. Clone the message first (structuredClone) when a test needs to compare pre-send state.
  • getSentMessages() returns a shallow copy. Mutating the returned array is safe (the store is unaffected), but the entries inside are shared.
  • The memory backend never rejects. result.rejected is always empty and send() never throws; use the failing stub above for error-path tests, or the retry stub from Pattern 5.

Pattern 5: Resilient Sends with Bounded Retries ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • Sending mail is part of a critical flow (password resets, order confirmations) and a transient SMTP hiccup should not lose the message.
  • You want predictable failure behavior: bounded attempts, observable retries, and one final error.
  • You want to combine the package's two error-reporting channels: send() throws on failure, while health() returns a boolean and never throws.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import {
    SmtpMailProvider,
    type MailMessage,
    type MailProvider,
    type MailResult,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

interface RetryOptions {
    /** Total send attempts, including the first. Default: 3 */
    maxAttempts?: number;
    /** Base backoff in milliseconds; doubles after each failure. Default: 500 */
    baseDelayMs?: number;
    /** Called after every failed attempt — wire this to your logger or metrics. */
    onAttemptFailed?: (attempt: number, error: Error) => void;
}

/** Sleep helper for backoff between attempts. */
function delay(ms: number): Promise<void> {
    return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

/**
 * Send a message with a pre-flight health check and bounded exponential
 * backoff. `send()` throws on SMTP failures, so every attempt is wrapped;
 * `health()` never throws and short-circuits the whole operation when the
 * backend is unreachable.
 */
async function sendWithRetry(
    provider: MailProvider,
    message: MailMessage,
    options: RetryOptions = {}
): Promise<MailResult> {
    const { maxAttempts = 3, baseDelayMs = 500, onAttemptFailed } = options;

    const healthy = await provider.health();
    if (!healthy) {
        throw new Error(`Mail provider "${provider.serviceName}" is not reachable`);
    }

    let lastError = new Error("No send attempt was performed");

    for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
        try {
            return await provider.send(message);
        } catch (error) {
            lastError = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
            onAttemptFailed?.(attempt, lastError);

            if (attempt < maxAttempts) {
                // Exponential backoff: baseDelayMs, 2x, 4x, ...
                await delay(baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
            }
        }
    }

    throw new Error(
        `Giving up after ${maxAttempts} attempts: ${lastError.message}`,
        { cause: lastError }
    );
}

const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    secure: false,
    auth: { user: "user@example.com", pass: "secret" },
});

try {
    const result = await sendWithRetry(
        mailer,
        {
            from: "noreply@example.com",
            to: "customer@example.com",
            subject: "Password reset",
            text: "Use code 482913 to reset your password.",
        },
        {
            maxAttempts: 3,
            baseDelayMs: 500,
            onAttemptFailed: (attempt, error) => {
                console.warn(`SMTP attempt ${attempt} failed: ${error.message}`);
            },
        }
    );

    console.log("Delivered to:", result.accepted);
} catch (error) {
    const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown error";
    console.error("Reset email could not be sent:", reason);
}

await mailer.shutdown();

Since the memory backend never throws, exercise the retry wrapper with a flaky stub in your tests:

typescript
// Stub for exercising the retry wrapper: fails twice, then succeeds.
class FlakyMailProvider extends MailProvider {
    private attempts = 0;

    async send(message: MailMessage): Promise<MailResult> {
        this.attempts += 1;
        if (this.attempts < 3) {
            throw new Error(`Transient SMTP failure #${this.attempts}`);
        }

        const recipients = Array.isArray(message.to) ? message.to : [message.to];
        return {
            accepted: recipients,
            rejected: [],
            messageId: `<flaky-${this.attempts}@test>`,
        };
    }

    async health(): Promise<boolean> {
        return true;
    }

    async shutdown(): Promise<void> {
        this.attempts = 0;
    }
}

Why This Pattern Matters ​

MailProvider reports trouble through two distinct channels, and this pattern uses both for what they are good at:

ChannelSemanticsBest Used For
health()Never throws; returns false when the backend is unreachableFail fast before attempting work; alerting and dashboards
send()Throws on connection, authentication, or send failuresWrapping in retries; propagating a final, actionable error

The retry wrapper is backend-agnostic — it types against MailProvider, so it works with SMTP, memory, or any custom provider, and on the memory backend it simply never retries.

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • SMTP is not exactly-once. A timeout after the server accepted a message can duplicate it on retry. Keep maxAttempts small and the backoff meaningful; for strict delivery guarantees, put an outbox/queue in front (this package deliberately does not provide one).
  • health() costs a network round trip. SmtpMailProvider.health() runs transporter.verify() — a real EHLO/HELO handshake, not a memory read. Do one pre-flight check as shown; never call it inside the retry loop, and see Pattern 7 for caching it.
  • Retries after shutdown() are pointless. Once the transport is closed, every send() fails; ordering teardown after in-flight work is Pattern 7's job.
  • rejected is not an error. A successful send() can still report recipients in result.rejected; retrying the whole message will not help those addresses.

Pattern 6: Batch Fan-Out with Per-Recipient Accounting ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • Sending personalized notifications to a list — order updates, account alerts, per-user digest content.
  • You need per-recipient bookkeeping: what was accepted, what was rejected, and what errored.
  • You must avoid both sequential slowness and unbounded concurrency.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import {
    SmtpMailProvider,
    type MailMessage,
    type MailProvider,
    type MailResult,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

interface Notification {
    recipient: string;
    orderId: string;
}

interface BatchReport {
    delivered: string[];
    rejected: string[];
    failed: Array<{ recipient: string; reason: string }>;
}

interface SendOutcome {
    notification: Notification;
    result: MailResult | null;
    error: Error | null;
}

/**
 * Send personalized notifications in small concurrent chunks.
 * Chunking keeps the connection pool busy without flooding the
 * SMTP server with hundreds of simultaneous sessions.
 */
async function sendShipmentNotifications(
    provider: MailProvider,
    notifications: Notification[],
    chunkSize = 5
): Promise<BatchReport> {
    const report: BatchReport = { delivered: [], rejected: [], failed: [] };

    for (let index = 0; index < notifications.length; index += chunkSize) {
        const chunk = notifications.slice(index, index + chunkSize);

        const outcomes: SendOutcome[] = await Promise.all(
            chunk.map(async (notification): Promise<SendOutcome> => {
                const message: MailMessage = {
                    from: "orders@example.com",
                    to: notification.recipient,
                    subject: `Order ${notification.orderId} has shipped`,
                    text: `Hello! Order ${notification.orderId} is on its way.`,
                };

                try {
                    return { notification, result: await provider.send(message), error: null };
                } catch (error) {
                    return {
                        notification,
                        result: null,
                        error: error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error)),
                    };
                }
            })
        );

        for (const outcome of outcomes) {
            if (outcome.error !== null) {
                report.failed.push({
                    recipient: outcome.notification.recipient,
                    reason: outcome.error.message,
                });
                continue;
            }

            if (outcome.result !== null) {
                if (outcome.result.accepted.includes(outcome.notification.recipient)) {
                    report.delivered.push(outcome.notification.recipient);
                }
                for (const address of outcome.result.rejected) {
                    report.rejected.push(address);
                }
            }
        }
    }

    return report;
}

const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    secure: false,
});

const report = await sendShipmentNotifications(mailer, [
    { recipient: "alice@example.com", orderId: "1001" },
    { recipient: "bob@example.com", orderId: "1002" },
    { recipient: "charlie@example.com", orderId: "1003" },
    { recipient: "dave@example.com", orderId: "1004" },
    { recipient: "erin@example.com", orderId: "1005" },
    { recipient: "frank@example.com", orderId: "1006" },
]);

console.log(`Delivered: ${report.delivered.length}`);
console.log(`Rejected: ${report.rejected.length}`);
console.log(`Failed: ${report.failed.length}`);

await mailer.shutdown();

When the content is identical for everyone, the cheaper variant is one message with array recipients — a single SMTP transaction with per-address accounting:

typescript
// Identical content? One message, one SMTP transaction, per-address results:
const result = await mailer.send({
    from: "news@example.com",
    to: ["subscriber-1@example.com", "subscriber-2@example.com", "subscriber-3@example.com"],
    subject: "Version 2.0 is out",
    text: "Here is what is new.",
});

console.log(result.accepted); // addresses the server took
console.log(result.rejected); // addresses the server refused

Why This Pattern Matters ​

  • Auditable delivery reports. MailResult.accepted / rejected plus per-send error capture produce a report you can log, persist, or show to an operator. Wrap each individual send in the retry helper from Pattern 5 when delivery matters more than batch latency.
  • Bounded concurrency, by design. Chunked Promise.all keeps throughput high while respecting the receiving server's tolerance — the nodemailer transport pools connections, but relays enforce rate limits and session caps of their own.
  • Backend-agnostic bookkeeping. The whole routine types against MailProvider, so the same code and the same unit tests run against the memory backend in CI.

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • accepted means "the server accepted the transaction" — not "the mailbox received it". Asynchronous bounces arrive later and are outside this package's scope.
  • Recipient visibility. Array to exposes the address list to every recipient; use bcc for hidden lists, or fan out personalized sends (as in the main example).
  • Tune chunk size to the relay. Start at 5 and adjust; large parallel bursts can trigger throttling or greylisting. Promise.all inside a chunk means one slow send delays the whole chunk — acceptable for mail, not for latency-critical work.
  • Large batches belong in a background job. Keep the fan-out out of synchronous HTTP request paths; the memory backend makes the surrounding logic fully unit-testable without SMTP.

Pattern 7: Standalone Lifecycle Management ​

When to Use This Pattern ​

  • Running the mailer in a standalone Node service (no WebAFX) — the documented use case for using providers directly.
  • The process receives SIGTERM/SIGINT (containers, Kubernetes) and must close the SMTP pool without dropping in-flight sends.
  • You expose health information but want to avoid a handshake round trip on every probe.

Complete Example ​

typescript
import {
    SmtpMailProvider,
    type MailMessage,
    type MailResult,
} from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    secure: false,
    auth: { user: "user@example.com", pass: "secret" },
});

/** In-flight sends — drained before the transport is closed. */
const inFlight = new Set<Promise<MailResult>>();

let shuttingDown = false;

/** Guarded send wrapper — refuses new work once shutdown has begun. */
async function send(message: MailMessage): Promise<MailResult> {
    if (shuttingDown) {
        throw new Error(`Mailer "${mailer.serviceName}" is shutting down`);
    }

    const pending = mailer.send(message);
    inFlight.add(pending);
    try {
        return await pending;
    } finally {
        inFlight.delete(pending);
    }
}

/** Idempotent teardown — drains in-flight sends, then closes the transport once. */
async function shutdown(): Promise<void> {
    if (shuttingDown) {
        return;
    }
    shuttingDown = true;

    await Promise.allSettled([...inFlight]);
    await mailer.shutdown();
    console.log("Mailer drained and transport closed");
}

for (const signal of ["SIGTERM", "SIGINT"] as const) {
    process.once(signal, () => {
        void shutdown().then(() => process.exit(0));
    });
}

// Application code uses the guarded wrapper instead of the provider directly:
const result = await send({
    from: "orders@example.com",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Order shipped",
    text: "Your order is on its way.",
});

console.log("Delivered to:", result.accepted);

// In a real service the process exits via the signal handlers;
// for this example, close explicitly (shutdown is idempotent):
await shutdown();

Because SmtpMailProvider.health() performs a real EHLO/HELO handshake (transporter.verify()), cache the result instead of calling it per probe:

typescript
// Cache the handshake — health() is a network round trip, not a memory read.
let healthy = false;
let checkedAt = 0;
const HEALTH_TTL_MS = 15_000;

async function isMailHealthy(): Promise<boolean> {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - checkedAt >= HEALTH_TTL_MS) {
        healthy = await mailer.health();
        checkedAt = now;
    }
    return healthy;
}

Why This Pattern Matters ​

  • Providers own resources. The SMTP provider holds a pooled set of TCP connections; shutdown() releases them, and an abrupt process exit can drop messages mid-send. Container platforms terminate processes with SIGTERM as a matter of routine — deploys should not lose password-reset emails.
  • Deterministic behavior at the boundary. The shuttingDown guard fails new sends fast with a clear error while the in-flight set drains existing work, so there is no window where a send starts against a closing transport.
  • Idempotency matches the plugin contract. The WebAFX plugin wires provider.shutdown() into both the singleton's dispose hook and its shutdown hook, so built-in providers are designed to tolerate repeated calls; the same discipline in standalone code keeps behavior consistent across deployment styles (and mirrors the lifecycle contract shared with blendsdk/webafx-cache's CacheProvider design).
  • Cheap health checks. Caching health() keeps /health endpoints honest without paying a handshake on every poll.

Caveats and Performance Notes ​

  • Installing signal handlers transfers exit responsibility to you. Call process.exit() after cleanup or let the event loop drain naturally; a handler that never exits turns a deploy into a hang.
  • Draining is best-effort. If deploy latency matters, bound the drain with a timeout (Promise.race against a timer) so a stuck SMTP connection cannot block termination forever.
  • After shutdown(), the provider is unusable. Subsequent send() calls fail; create a new provider if the work must continue.
  • Cache with a TTL, not forever. A cached true can mask a failure that occurs between checks; 10–30 seconds is a reasonable range for health endpoints, and Pattern 5's pre-flight check covers the send path itself.

webafx-mailer Best Practices ​

blendsdk/webafx-mailer is a deliberately small package — one abstract contract (MailProvider), two interchangeable backends, and a thin WebAFX adapter — and almost every mistake with it is a lifecycle or contract mistake: providers created too often, never shut down, health checks placed in hot paths, or test helpers hidden behind one-liners. This document pairs each practice with the approach it replaces, then collects the recurring anti-patterns, performance tips, and security notes.

Do / Don't Pairs ​

Each pair contrasts the problematic approach (❌ Wrong) with the recommended one (✅ Correct), followed by the reasoning. Pairs are numbered so the Quick Reference and cross-references line up.

1. Program against MailProvider, not a concrete backend ​

❌ Wrong — depend on SmtpMailProvider:

typescript
import { SmtpMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Business logic is welded to one backend: every test of this function
// now needs a real SMTP server.
async function sendPasswordReset(mailer: SmtpMailProvider, to: string): Promise<void> {
    await mailer.send({
        from: "noreply@example.com",
        to,
        subject: "Reset your password",
        text: "Use the link in this email to reset your password.",
    });
}

✅ Correct — depend on the abstract type:

typescript
import type { MailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Any backend fits: SmtpMailProvider in production, MemoryMailProvider in
// tests, a custom subclass anywhere else.
async function sendPasswordReset(mailer: MailProvider, to: string): Promise<void> {
    await mailer.send({
        from: "noreply@example.com",
        to,
        subject: "Reset your password",
        text: "Use the link in this email to reset your password.",
    });
}

Why: backend interchangeability is the core design of the package — SmtpMailProvider, MemoryMailProvider, and custom subclasses all satisfy the same three-method contract, and createMailPlugin() accepts any of them. Typing against a concrete class re-couples every call site to one delivery mechanism, forces tests onto the network, and turns backend swapping into a refactoring project instead of a one-line composition change.

2. Create one provider per application — never per send ​

❌ Wrong — construct a transport for every email:

typescript
import { SmtpMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

async function notifyCustomer(message: MailMessage): Promise<void> {
    // Fresh transport per call: full connection setup every time,
    // and the previous transport is never closed.
    const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({ host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587 });
    await mailer.send(message);
}

✅ Correct — compose once, reuse everywhere:

typescript
import { SmtpMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Created once at the composition root and reused for the process lifetime.
const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({ host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587 });

async function notifyCustomer(message: MailMessage): Promise<void> {
    await mailer.send(message); // reuses the transport's connection handling
}

Why: a provider wraps exactly one nodemailer transport, and that transport is built to be long-lived — it manages connection pooling internally and only releases it via shutdown(). A provider-per-send throws that away, performs a fresh connection setup for every message, and leaks the abandoned transport. This is precisely why the WebAFX plugin registers the provider as an application-wide singleton service.

3. Shut down every provider you create ​

❌ Wrong — abandon the transport when you are done:

typescript
const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({ host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587 });
await mailer.send(notification);
// No shutdown: the transport and its pooled connections are left for the GC.

✅ Correct — call shutdown() when the provider's job is done:

typescript
import { SmtpMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({ host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587 });

try {
    await mailer.send(notification);
} finally {
    await mailer.shutdown(); // closes the transport / connection pool
}

Why: shutdown() is the package's terminal lifecycle call — on SMTP it closes the nodemailer transport and its connection pool; on the memory backend it clears the store. After calling it, subsequent send() calls fail, so treat it as final. The WebAFX plugin wires shutdown() into graceful application disposal for exactly this reason; standalone code must call it itself, and test suites should call it in afterEach (the package's own tests do).

4. Handle send() failures — SMTP throws, it does not return a status ​

❌ Wrong — assume every send resolves:

typescript
// Connection refused, bad credentials, or a send rejection — all of these
// reject the promise; nothing here notices.
await mailer.send(receipt);
markOrderAsNotified(orderId);

✅ Correct — catch, log the reason, and decide deliberately:

typescript
import type { MailMessage, MailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

async function deliver(mailer: MailProvider, message: MailMessage): Promise<boolean> {
    try {
        await mailer.send(message);
        return true;
    } catch (error) {
        const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown SMTP failure";
        console.error(`Email delivery failed: ${reason}`);
        return false; // caller decides: retry, alert, or surface to the user
    }
}

Why: SmtpMailProvider.send() rejects on connection failures, authentication failures, and send rejections — failure is always signalled by throwing, never by a boolean or status field. The memory backend never throws, which makes it an excellent test double but a dangerous way to discover missing error handling: code paths exercised only against MemoryMailProvider will never hit the catch branch, so review send sites explicitly.

5. Use health() for monitoring, not as a per-send precondition ​

❌ Wrong — gate every send behind a health check:

typescript
// verify() opens a connection and performs an EHLO/HELO handshake;
// then send() performs its own full connection sequence again.
if (await mailer.health()) {
    await mailer.send(message);
}

✅ Correct — let send() fail fast; poll health() where it belongs:

typescript
import { createMailPlugin } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Register once — the plugin wires health() into the application's /health endpoint.
app.use(createMailPlugin(mailer));

// Hot paths call send() directly — connection problems surface as rejections.
await mailer.send(message);

Why: health() on the SMTP backend calls nodemailer's verify(), a full connection handshake performed without sending email. Using it as a gate roughly doubles the connection-setup work per message and still proves nothing about the next call — the server can fail between the check and the send, and send() already fails fast on its own. The plugin layer exists so health() can be polled on a schedule (health endpoints, readiness probes) independently of traffic.

6. In tests, wrap a MemoryMailProvider you own — don't hide it behind the one-liner ​

❌ Wrong — memoryMailPlugin() when the test needs assertions:

typescript
import { memoryMailPlugin } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// The provider instance lives and dies inside the plugin factory —
// there is no reference to call getSentMessages() or getLastMessage() on.
app.use(memoryMailPlugin());

✅ Correct — create the provider first, then adapt it:

typescript
import { createMailPlugin, MemoryMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

const mailer = new MemoryMailProvider({ serviceName: "mailer" });
app.use(createMailPlugin(mailer));

// After the code under test has run, assert against the captured store:
expect(mailer.getSentMessages()).toHaveLength(1);
expect(mailer.getLastMessage()?.message.subject).toBe("Welcome!");

Why: memoryMailPlugin() constructs the provider internally and keeps the reference private — ideal for smoke setups, useless for assertions. createMailPlugin() adapts any provider you hand it, so owning the instance keeps the full test-helper surface (getSentMessages, getLastMessage, clear) available while still registering it as the application-wide singleton.

7. Reset the memory store between test cases ​

❌ Wrong — one shared store across the whole file:

typescript
// Module-level provider shared by every test: counts and "last message"
// assertions now depend on execution order.
const mailer = new MemoryMailProvider();

it("captures one welcome email", async () => {
    await mailer.send(welcome);
    expect(mailer.getSentMessages()).toHaveLength(1); // passes — for now
});

it("captures one reminder email", async () => {
    await mailer.send(reminder);
    expect(mailer.getSentMessages()).toHaveLength(1); // fails: 2 entries
});

✅ Correct — a fresh provider (or explicit reset) per test:

typescript
import { MemoryMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

let mailer: MemoryMailProvider;

beforeEach(() => {
    mailer = new MemoryMailProvider();
});

afterEach(async () => {
    await mailer.shutdown(); // clears the store and releases resources
});

Why: the memory provider's store is append-only — nothing is discarded until clear() or shutdown() is called. A shared instance (or a provider registered as a singleton in a long-lived test app) accumulates messages across cases, so getSentMessages() lengths and getLastMessage() assertions silently depend on test order. The package's own memory tests create a fresh provider in beforeEach and shut it down in afterEach, and its SMTP tests clear the receiving server between cases — apply the same isolation discipline to your tests.

8. Treat messageId as optional ​

❌ Wrong — non-null assertion to silence the contract:

typescript
const result = await mailer.send(message);
const id = result.messageId!; // compiles by force, not by contract
persistTransportId(id.toUpperCase());

✅ Correct — branch on presence:

typescript
import type { MailResult } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

function transportIdOf(result: MailResult): string {
    return result.messageId ?? "(no transport message id)";
}

const result = await mailer.send(message);
const id = transportIdOf(result);

Why: MailResult.messageId is deliberately optional so providers built on asynchronous APIs — the contract tests cite the Microsoft Graph style of "accepted without a transport identifier" — can satisfy the same interface. Both shipped backends populate it (SMTP from the server, memory with a synthetic <memory-…@test> value), but code that depends on the value breaks the moment a custom provider joins the mix. The package's own contract tests guard with if (result.messageId !== undefined); do the same instead of reaching for !.

9. After SMTP sends, inspect rejected — success is not all-or-nothing ​

❌ Wrong — assume the send covered every recipient:

typescript
await mailer.send({
    from: "noreply@example.com",
    to: ["alice@example.com", "bob@example.com"],
    subject: "Release notes",
    text: "Here is what changed.",
});
// Done — but bob's mailbox quota was exceeded and the server said so
// in result.rejected, which was discarded.

✅ Correct — check the outcome the server reported:

typescript
const result = await mailer.send({
    from: "noreply@example.com",
    to: ["alice@example.com", "bob@example.com"],
    subject: "Release notes",
    text: "Here is what changed.",
});

if (result.rejected.length > 0) {
    console.warn(`SMTP server rejected: ${result.rejected.join(", ")}`);
    // flag, retry, or clean up the affected addresses
}

Why: send() throws for transport-level failures, but the SMTP conversation itself can complete while individual recipients are refused (unknown mailbox, quota exceeded, policy blocks). Those addresses land in result.rejected — not in an exception — so code that only catches errors will believe delivery was complete. rejected exists on every backend (the memory backend always returns []), so inspecting it is portable across providers.

10. Set secure to match the port ​

❌ Wrong — implicit TLS on the STARTTLS port:

typescript
import { SmtpMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Port 587 expects plaintext plus a STARTTLS upgrade; secure: true demands
// TLS from the first byte — the connection hangs or fails.
const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    secure: true,
});

✅ Correct — use the pairings the defaults were designed around:

typescript
// Port 465 — implicit TLS from the first byte
const implicitTls = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 465,
    secure: true,
});

// Port 587 — STARTTLS (the default: secure defaults to false)
const starttls = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    secure: false,
});

Why: secure means "speak TLS immediately, before any SMTP dialogue" — correct for port 465, incorrect for 587, where the server expects a plaintext greeting that is then upgraded via STARTTLS. The provider defaults secure to false precisely because STARTTLS on 587 is the modern convention; only set it to true when the server genuinely uses implicit TLS.

11. Never fire-and-forget a send() ​

❌ Wrong — a floating promise:

typescript
// No await: a rejection becomes an unhandled rejection (process-fatal by
// default in modern Node) and the MailResult is lost.
mailer.send(notification);

✅ Correct — await it, or make background delivery explicit:

typescript
import type { MailMessage, MailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Option A — wait for the outcome.
await mailer.send(notification);

// Option B — deliberate background delivery with its own error handling.
async function sendInBackground(mailer: MailProvider, message: MailMessage): Promise<void> {
    try {
        await mailer.send(message);
    } catch (error) {
        const reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : "unknown failure";
        console.error(`Background email failed: ${reason}`);
    }
}

Why: send() returns a promise that can reject, and Node treats unhandled rejections as process-fatal by default. Fire-and-forget also discards MailResult — the only place partial rejections surface (see practice 9) — so even "successful" background sends lose their observability. If delivery should not block the caller, wrap it in a named, error-handled async function like Option B instead of dropping the promise.

12. Give each provider a distinct serviceName ​

❌ Wrong — two providers, one registration identity:

typescript
import { memoryMailPlugin, smtpMailPlugin } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// Both default to serviceName "mailer": the plugins collide by name and
// the second registration can shadow the first in the service container.
app.use(smtpMailPlugin({ host: "smtp.example.com", port: 587 }));
app.use(memoryMailPlugin());

✅ Correct — name every mailer:

typescript
app.use(smtpMailPlugin({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    serviceName: "transactional-mailer",
}));
app.use(memoryMailPlugin({ serviceName: "dev-mailer" }));

Why: serviceName is the provider's single identity — it becomes both the plugin's name and the service-container registration key. Colliding names make resolution order-dependent and ambiguous, while distinct names support multi-mailer setups (transactional vs. marketing mail), exactly as the configuration documentation suggests. The name is read from the config at construction time, so set it there.

13. Provide a text body next to html ​

❌ Wrong — HTML-only messages:

typescript
await mailer.send({
    from: "noreply@example.com",
    to: user.email,
    subject: "Your invoice",
    html: "<h1>Your invoice is attached.</h1>",
});

✅ Correct — both parts, as the message model intends:

typescript
await mailer.send({
    from: "noreply@example.com",
    to: user.email,
    subject: "Your invoice",
    text: "Your invoice is attached.",
    html: "<h1>Your invoice is attached.</h1>",
});

Why: MailMessage documents text as the fallback body "used when HTML is also provided" — supplying the pair is what makes rich-plus-plain delivery possible. Text-only clients, accessibility tooling, and many spam heuristics read the plain-text part; sending html alone degrades all of them. Both fields are individually optional, but the documented guidance is to provide at least one body — and both when you can.

Quick Reference ​

#PracticeDoDon't
1Dependency directionType against MailProviderConcrete SmtpMailProvider in business logic
2Provider lifetimeOne instance per app, reusedNew provider per send
3Teardownshutdown() on completion; afterEach in testsAbandon transports
4Failure handlingtry/catch around send(); log and decideAssume sends always resolve
5Health checksHealth endpoints / readiness probesPer-send precondition
6Test assertionsWrap your own MemoryMailProvider via createMailPlugin()memoryMailPlugin() when asserting
7Test isolationFresh provider or clear() per caseShared accumulating store
8messageIdOptional-check (??)Non-null assertion (!)
9rejectedInspect after SMTP sendsAssume all recipients accepted
10secureMatch port (465 → true, 587 → false)Mismatch port and TLS mode
11Background sendsAwait or explicit error-handled taskFire-and-forget promise
12Multi-mailerDistinct serviceName per providerColliding "mailer" defaults
13Message bodiestext + htmlhtml only

Anti-Patterns ​

These are the recurring integration mistakes, several of which the package's own tests and documentation explicitly steer away from.

Hand-rolled provider mocks instead of MemoryMailProvider ​

Teams sometimes stub the provider by hand — a minimal subclass or a fake object — instead of using the backend the package ships for exactly this purpose:

typescript
import { MailProvider, type MailMessage, type MailResult } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// ❌ Reimplementing a test backend by hand — drifts from the real contract.
class FakeMailer extends MailProvider {
    readonly sent: MailMessage[] = [];

    async send(message: MailMessage): Promise<MailResult> {
        this.sent.push(message);
        return { accepted: [], rejected: [] };
        // Does not match real semantics: the shipped memory backend puts
        // every to/cc/bcc address into accepted.
    }

    async health(): Promise<boolean> {
        return true;
    }

    async shutdown(): Promise<void> {
        this.sent.length = 0; // "close enough"
    }
}

MemoryMailProvider is this backend — contract-tested against the same suite as the SMTP provider. It normalizes to/cc/bcc into accepted, generates pattern-checked <memory-…@test> message IDs, protects its store from array mutation, and keeps identity semantics (toBe) working for assertions. A hand-rolled fake drifts the moment any of that matters: a fake returning accepted: [] passes your tests while the real backend reports recipients, and it can never tell you that your production code assumes health() throws.

Do this instead:

typescript
import { MemoryMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// ✅ The shipped backend already implements everything the fake tried to do.
const mailer = new MemoryMailProvider();

Constructing providers from unvalidated configuration ​

MailFactoryConfig makes the SMTP fields optional because they are only read when type === "smtp" — which means this compiles:

typescript
import { createMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// ❌ Compiles, but host/port may be undefined: the provider is created
// "successfully" and only fails on the first real send.
const mailer = createMailProvider({
    type: "smtp",
    host: process.env.SMTP_HOST,         // string | undefined
    port: Number(process.env.SMTP_PORT), // NaN when unset
});

The factory forwards these values straight into the transport — and as casts (type: value as "smtp") are worse, because they hide the very configuration mistakes the factory's runtime guard is designed to surface with a clear error.

Validate once, at startup, and fail fast:

typescript
import { createMailProvider, type MailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

function requireEnv(name: string): string {
    const value = process.env[name];
    if (value === undefined || value === "") {
        throw new Error(`Missing required environment variable: ${name}`);
    }
    return value;
}

const port = Number(requireEnv("SMTP_PORT"));
if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port <= 0) {
    throw new Error(`SMTP_PORT must be a positive integer, received "${process.env.SMTP_PORT}"`);
}

const mailer: MailProvider = createMailProvider({
    type: "smtp",
    host: requireEnv("SMTP_HOST"),
    port,
    serviceName: "transactional-mailer",
});

console.log(`Mail provider ready: ${mailer.serviceName}`);

A misconfigured process should refuse to start (or fall back deliberately) — never discover the problem on the first customer email.

The "temporary" memory backend in production ​

typescript
import { createMailPlugin, createMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// ❌ No email leaves the process: messages pile up in memory forever.
const mailer = createMailProvider({ type: "memory" });
app.use(createMailPlugin(mailer));

The memory backend never sends anything, retains full message payloads (recipients, bodies, attachments) in process memory until shutdown(), and grows without bound as a stand-in "outbox". In production, "temporary" tends to become permanent — and every email that should have reached a customer is silently captured instead.

Do this instead: make the environment choice explicit, the way the configuration documentation shows, and validate the SMTP fields at startup (see the previous anti-pattern) so production cannot accidentally fall into the memory branch:

typescript
// ✅ Explicit, environment-driven choice.
const mailer = createMailProvider({
    type: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production" ? "smtp" : "memory",
    host: process.env.SMTP_HOST,
    port: Number(process.env.SMTP_PORT ?? "587"),
});

Mutating message objects after send() ​

typescript
// ❌ The memory provider stores the message object by reference —
// mutating it later rewrites what getSentMessages() reports.
const message: MailMessage = { from, to, subject: "Order placed", text: "Thanks!" };

await mailer.send(message);
message.subject = "Order shipped"; // also changes the stored record

expect(mailer.getSentMessages()[0].message.subject).toBe("Order placed"); // fails

The memory provider deliberately stores the same object you passed so identity assertions (toBe) work — that is a feature for assertions and a trap for shared, mutable fixtures. Mutating a message after send corrupts earlier records and makes test failures depend on object reuse.

Do this instead: treat MailMessage objects as write-once. Build a fresh message per send, or spread immutable overrides:

typescript
const baseMessage: MailMessage = { from, to, text: "Thanks!" };

await mailer.send({ ...baseMessage, subject: "Order placed" });
await mailer.send({ ...baseMessage, subject: "Order shipped" });

Silent catch around send() ​

typescript
// ❌ Failure is known and discarded: no log, no retry, no signal.
try {
    await mailer.send(receipt);
} catch {
    // ignore
}

An empty catch converts actionable SMTP failures — expired credentials, quota exhaustion, network outages — into invisible data loss. Because the package intentionally ships no retry queue or outbox, "what happens when sending fails" is a decision your application must make; the empty catch makes that decision implicitly and badly.

Do this instead: at minimum log the error with context, then make the policy explicit — rethrow so the caller can react, hand off to your own retry/outbox mechanism, or record the failure for manual follow-up.

Asserting on SMTP delivery immediately after send() resolves ​

typescript
// ❌ Racy: send() completed, but the receiving system (a test mail server
// such as Mailpit, or any external sink) may not have indexed the message yet.
await mailer.send({ from, to, subject: "Race condition", text: "..." });
const received = await getMailpitMessages();
expect(received).toHaveLength(1); // flaky — empty now, stale later

Delivery to the SMTP server and observability of that delivery in the sink are two separate events; the naive assertion also trips over messages left behind by previous tests. The package's own integration tests solve both problems with a bounded polling helper that matches on a unique subject:

typescript
// ✅ Poll until the specific message appears (the package's tests allow up to
// 25 attempts at 200 ms), then assert on the matched message only.
async function waitForMessage(subject: string): Promise<MailpitMessage> {
    for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 25; attempt++) {
        const messages = await getMailpitMessages();
        const match = messages.find((m) => m.Subject === subject);
        if (match) return match;
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
    }
    throw new Error(`Timed out waiting for message "${subject}"`);
}

Do this instead: use unique subjects per test, clear the sink between tests, and poll with a bounded retry loop. Better yet, keep this style of test to a thin SMTP integration suite — unit tests should assert against MemoryMailProvider, where the message is stored synchronously and no polling is needed.

Performance Tips ​

The package's performance profile is dominated by one thing — how you manage the provider lifecycle — plus a handful of backend-specific wins.

Reuse one provider for the process lifetime ​

Each SmtpMailProvider owns one transport built for long-lived use: it manages its connection pooling internally, and shutdown() is the documented way to release it. A provider-per-send pays full connection setup (TCP + TLS + authentication) per message and abandons transports. The plugin layer registers providers as singletons for the same reason — reuse is the performance model.

Keep health() off the send path ​

On SMTP, health() runs verify() — a complete connect + EHLO/HELO handshake performed without sending mail. Called before each send, it roughly doubles the connection-setup work per email and adds no safety (the check is inherently racy, and send() fails fast on its own). Schedule health() from your health endpoint or a readiness probe instead; one probe interval is plenty for monitoring.

Batch recipients into one message ​

to/cc/bcc accept arrays, and a single send() with N recipients is one SMTP transaction instead of N. For small groups, list everyone directly; when recipients should not see each other, put the batch in bcc. Real-world servers cap recipients per message, so chunk very large audiences (newsletter scale) across multiple sends.

Prefer Buffer attachment content over base64 strings ​

MailAttachment.content accepts Buffer | string; the string form is base64, which carries roughly 33% size overhead versus the binary data and requires a decode step in the transport. Use Buffer whenever the content is already binary (a file read, a generated PDF); use base64 only when that is the form you were handed.

Use the memory backend in development and CI ​

MemoryMailProvider.send() is a synchronous array push — no network, no Docker, no flakiness. The package's unit tests run with it and need no infrastructure at all; only the SMTP integration suite requires the Mailpit container. Mirror that split: unit and most integration tests against the memory backend, a thin SMTP suite for wire-level confidence.

Bound the memory store in long-lived processes ​

The memory backend's store is append-only: every captured message — including attachments — stays in memory until clear() or shutdown(). In tests that is a feature; in a long-running dev server it is a slow leak. Call clear() on a schedule (or after assertions) when the process handles many messages.

Shut down promptly — especially in tests ​

shutdown() closes the transport pool (SMTP) or clears the store (memory). Test suites that create a provider per case and skip shutdown() accumulate pooled sockets across the run — the package's own suites put shutdown in afterEach for exactly this reason. For SMTP, a graceful close also lets the server release its session immediately instead of waiting for a timeout. Remember that post-shutdown sends fail, so shut down only when the provider is genuinely done.

Security Considerations ​

Keep TLS certificate validation enabled ​

The provider deliberately ships no hardcoded tls.rejectUnauthorized: false — validation is on by default, and the tls config option exists so you can relax it, not so you should. Disabling validation lets any on-path attacker impersonate the SMTP server and harvest credentials and message contents.

typescript
// ❌ Disables verification in ALL environments — man-in-the-middle territory.
new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    tls: { rejectUnauthorized: false },
});

// ✅ Keep the default (verify). Relax only against a local development
// server with a self-signed certificate, never for internet-facing SMTP.
new SmtpMailProvider({ host: "localhost", port: 1025, secure: false });

Source credentials from the environment, never from source ​

SmtpMailConfig.auth is a plaintext { user, pass }. Keep it out of the repository, out of source files, and out of logs — pass it from environment variables or a secret manager at startup:

typescript
import { SmtpMailProvider } from "blendsdk/webafx-mailer";

// ✅ Secrets arrive at runtime; the source tree contains none.
const user = process.env.SMTP_USER;
const pass = process.env.SMTP_PASS;
if (!user || !pass) {
    throw new Error("SMTP_USER and SMTP_PASS must be set");
}

const mailer = new SmtpMailProvider({
    host: "smtp.example.com",
    port: 587,
    auth: { user, pass },
});

Also note what not to log: configuration objects (they carry auth.pass) and message bodies. The plugin's initialization log deliberately records only the service name and the provider class — keep your custom logging at the same level of restraint.

Use TLS-capable ports so credentials and content are protected in transit ​

Port 465 wraps the entire session in TLS; port 587 performs a STARTTLS upgrade before authenticated delivery; port 25 is designed for server-to-server relay and is rarely the right choice for application mail with credentials. Pair the port with the correct secure value (see practice 10) and keep certificate validation on (above) — an encrypted connection whose certificate is never verified provides confidentiality against passive observers only.

Treat MailResult.accepted as sensitive ​

accepted reflects the envelope recipients: on the memory backend it is to + cc + bcc flattened; on SMTP it maps the server's envelope response. That means BCC addresses — recipients deliberately hidden from the visible headers — can appear in it. Do not log result.accepted wholesale or ship it to third-party analytics; log counts, or mask addresses, if you must record the outcome.

Keep the memory backend out of production ​

MemoryMailProvider retains every message's full payload — recipients, subjects, bodies, attachments — in plain process memory for the life of the provider. That is ideal for tests and wrong for production: besides sending nothing (see the anti-pattern above), it means PII and potentially sensitive documents sit in memory until the next clear() or shutdown().

Validate untrusted input before it becomes email content ​

Addresses, display names, and subjects frequently originate from end users or upstream systems. Pass them through the typed MailMessage fields rather than assembling raw header strings by concatenation, apply basic sanity checks at the boundary (address shape, length caps), and normalize user input to a single line for fields such as subject. Cheap validation up front prevents malformed headers and header-splitting style abuses from ever reaching the transport.
